analysis.one_liner: Replaces the income, payroll, and estate taxes with a 23% national sales tax.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 70 cosponsors but never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the Ways and Means Committee, and it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Tax Act would repeal the federal income tax, payroll taxes, and estate and gift taxes, and replace them with a single national sales tax of 23% on nearly everything people buy (measured tax-inclusive, that adds roughly 30% at the register). Every registered family would get a monthly rebate covering the tax on purchases up to the poverty line, and states would collect the tax for a fee. The IRS would be defunded by 2015, and the sales tax would shut itself off if the constitutional amendment permitting an income tax were not repealed within seven years.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most: their income, capital gains, and payroll tax bills disappear, purchases made for investment are exempt, and the estate tax is repealed. All workers gain from an end to payroll withholding, and low- and middle-income families gain protection through the monthly poverty-level rebate.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the income tax, Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate and gift taxes, effective January 1, 2013 [S2, S3].
Gives every registered family a monthly rebate equal to the sales tax rate times the federal poverty level, so households at or below poverty pay no net sales tax [S2, S3].
Exempts from the tax anything purchased for business, investment, or export purposes, and taxes only final consumption [S2, S3].
Prohibits funding for the IRS after fiscal year 2015 and ends individual income tax filing [S2, S3].
Ends payroll withholding, so workers receive their full wages before any consumption tax is paid [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers, especially middle-income households, who would pay the 23% tax (about 30% added at the register) on nearly everything they buy; their consumption is a larger share of their income than it is for high earners, whose savings and investment income go untaxed.

drawbacks.text: The 23% rate is applied to gross payments including the tax itself, meaning an effective markup of roughly 30% on top of shelf prices for most goods and services [S3].

Because a consumption tax falls hardest on households that spend most of their income, and purchases for investment are exempt, the tax burden shifts away from income earned on wealth and toward wages spent on living costs [S2, S3].

Receiving the rebate requires annual family registration with Social Security numbers, certification of lawful residency, and signed filings; families that fail to register on time lose the rebate for months [S3].

The bill sets a fixed 14.91% general-revenue rate plus fixed rates for the Social Security and Medicare trust funds, with no mechanism proving the combined rate raises the same revenue as the taxes it repeals [S2, S3].

The sales tax would terminate if the Sixteenth Amendment (the income tax amendment) is not repealed within seven years, leaving a transition risk between the old system's repeal and the constitutional change [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who hate filing taxes and distrust the IRS, the trade is real: no income tax, no payroll withholding, no annual filing, and a rebate that fully offsets the tax for the poorest families. But the core bargain is a shift: taxes currently paid on income, capital gains, and large estates move onto consumption. Households that save and invest a large share of income end up paying far less than they do today, while households that spend nearly everything they earn pay the full rate on every purchase. The rebate softens this at the bottom, but the middle class — not the wealthy — carries the heaviest new burden. Independent analysts have long disputed whether the stated 23% rate could actually be revenue-neutral, and the bill builds in a seven-year sunset precisely because many supporters and critics alike feared a consumption tax layered on top of an unrepealed income tax.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress expired two years later.

narrative.text: Rep. Rob Woodall (R-GA) introduced the Fair Tax Act of 2011 on January 5, 2011 [S1, S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
It gathered 70 cosponsors — 69 Republicans and 1 Democrat — the largest cosponsor count of any tax reform proposal of that era [S4].
No further action was ever recorded: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action, through January 3, 2013, when the 112th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No new group gained, because the bill never advanced. The existing tax code — including income taxes on investment, payroll taxes, and the estate tax — remained in place, which is the outcome opponents of the consumption-tax shift preferred. Supporters of the IRS's abolition and repeal of taxes on wealth lost their best-organized vehicle of that Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: the tax code stayed intact

for.name: Rep. Rob Woodall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 5, 2011 and shepherded it as lead sponsor.

for.name: 69 of 242 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including a bloc of original cosponsors led by members from Georgia and the bill's long-time House backers [S3, S4].

for.name: 1 of 193 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it nominally bipartisan.

for.name: Americans for Fair Taxation and FairTax grassroots activists
for.what_they_did: Sustained a national advocacy campaign for the FairTax proposal across multiple Congresses, including this one.

against.name: Rep. Dave Camp
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the committee recorded no action on it for the entire two-year Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Republican: 69 of the 70 cosponsors were Republicans, with one Democrat (Rep. Dan Boren) joining [S4].

industries.industry: High-income households, investors, and large estates
industries.note: The bill repeals the income tax on capital gains and other investment income, exempts investment purchases from the sales tax, and repeals the estate and gift tax entirely [S2, S3]. Those gains come directly out of the taxes that middle-income wage earners and consumers would instead pay through the 23% sales tax on everything they buy.

industries.industry: Retailers and sellers of goods and services
industries.note: Retailers would have to register, collect, segregate, and remit the tax monthly with penalties for failure [S3]. They would receive a taxpayer administration credit of at least $200 or 0.25% of tax remitted per month to offset the cost [S3].

States with existing sales taxes would become the permanent federal collection channel, remitting revenue to the Treasury and keeping a 0.25% administration fee, with a new federal Office of Revenue Allocation arbitrating disputes [S2, S3].

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax compliance services
industries.note: Repealing the income tax and defunding the IRS after FY2015 eliminates the annual filing compliance industry that serves individuals [S2].

Intangible property — securities, bonds, and other financial instruments — is exempt from the tax, and investment purchases go untaxed, a major benefit to the sector's clients [S3]. However, fees for financial intermediation services are explicitly taxed [S3].
